sections.heading: Depending on you alone
sections.text: My dear Lord, I am completely dependent on you. Please loosen my grip on every other thing I lean on as if it could hold me up. You are enough for me. You rule over everything, and you have set your love on me. Teach my heart to live like that is true.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God himself is his highest treasure and strength when everything else fails. That directly supports the prayer’s movement away from false supports and toward God as the believer’s all.
Paul describes God as the one who works all things according to his will. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that God rules over every circumstance, not merely religious parts of life.

sections.heading: Trusting your goodness instead of living anxious
sections.text: You are the source of every good thing. So why do I keep distrusting you? Why do I let fear take over when I do not know what will happen next? Help me remember who you are before I react to what I can see.
theological_themes: God as the fountain of goodness

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every good and perfect gift comes from God, whose character does not shift. This supports the prayer’s appeal to God’s goodness as the reason distrust is unreasonable.

Jesus calls his disciples away from anxiety by pointing them to the Father’s knowledge and care. The prayer echoes that logic: God’s goodness and fatherly rule are meant to quiet fear about what may happen.

sections.heading: Seeing everything else in the light of your worth
sections.text: When I see how precious you are, the world’s pleasures look small and poor. Even the approval of people is no treasure compared with your favor. Keep me from building my life around being noticed, praised, admired, or secure in earthly comforts.
theological_themes: freedom from the fear of man

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts former gains as loss because knowing Christ is of surpassing worth. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s claim that worldly enjoyments and status become small in comparison with God.
Paul contrasts seeking human approval with being a servant of Christ. This supports the prayer’s rejection of living for the favor of people.

sections.heading: Loving you in the gifts without forgetting the Giver
sections.text: Father, when you bless me, do not let my heart become like a stranger toward you. Let every good thing lead me back to you with love, not away from you in pride or forgetfulness. I know my greatest dangers may come through my comforts, successes, and advantages, because I can start trusting them instead of you.
theological_themes: love for the Giver above the gifts

scripture_references.connection: Moses warns Israel that prosperity can lead them to forget the Lord and imagine their strength produced their blessings. This closely matches the prayer’s concern that advantages can become spiritually dangerous.
Paul commands the rich not to set their hope on uncertain riches but on God, who richly provides. The passage supports receiving benefits from God without letting them replace him.

sections.heading: Letting my emptiness make Christ precious
sections.text: Bring me to the end of confidence in myself, not so I sink into despair without hope, but so Jesus becomes deeply precious to me. Let me gladly receive him as my Savior, my Lord, my wisdom, my righteousness, my strength, and my way to you. Make his path beautiful to me. Teach me to love his commands, not only his promises.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says Christ becomes wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for believers, leaving no room for boasting in ourselves. This grounds the prayer’s request that self-despair would make Christ precious in all his saving work.
Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This supports the prayer’s rejection of self-reliance and its turning to Christ as the believer’s life and strength.
Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments. The prayer’s desire to love Christ’s commands as well as his promises reflects this biblical connection between affection and obedience.

sections.heading: Learning the difference between true love and selfish religion
sections.text: Please teach me the difference between real love for you and a false love that only uses you for what I want. True love puts you above everything. It joins your glory and my good together, because my happiness is found in you being honored and loved. False love separates them; it wants my benefit while neglecting your glory. Give me grace to recognize the difference in my own heart.
theological_themes: God’s glory and human joy held together

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies love for God with the whole heart, soul, and mind as the greatest commandment. This supports the prayer’s definition of true love as supreme love for God rather than merely self-interested religion.
Paul teaches that even ordinary actions should be done for God’s glory. This grounds the prayer’s concern that human happiness must not be pursued apart from God’s honor.
The psalm locates fullness of joy in God’s presence. This supports the prayer’s claim that God’s glory and the believer’s deepest happiness are not enemies but belong together.

sections.heading: Resting in you, the God who is love
sections.text: Make my love for you more than a conclusion I can argue for, and more than a bargain for my own advantage. Let it become a real affection awakened by your love, bringing honest joy to my mind and heart. Give me grace to recognize what is genuine and what is fake, and let me rest in you, because you are love.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that love comes from God, that God is love, and that believers love because God first loved them. This directly supports the prayer’s longing for genuine love rooted in God’s own loving nature.

Jesus speaks of abiding in his love, keeping his commandments, and receiving his joy. This connects love, obedience, and joy in the way the prayer asks for love that is living and pleasurable, not merely theoretical.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The phrase “self-despair” could be misunderstood today as hopelessness or self-hatred. I rendered it as coming to the end of self-confidence, while preserving the original Puritan emphasis that Christ becomes precious when self-reliance is exposed.

The original contrasts true love for God with love motivated by rational argument or self-interest. I preserved the distinction, but avoided implying that Christian love is irrational; the point is that genuine love is more than calculation, proof, or personal advantage.

The prayer’s claim that a person’s “greatest danger” may arise from advantages reflects a biblical warning about prosperity and comfort, but it can sound absolute. I rendered it as a serious spiritual danger through comforts, successes, and advantages.
significant_interpretive_choices: “All his offices” was interpreted as Christ’s full saving sufficiency—his work as Savior, Lord, wisdom, righteousness, strength, and way to the Father—rather than listing the traditional threefold office in technical terms.
“The heart of a stranger” was rendered as becoming distant and forgetful toward God while enjoying his blessings, since the phrase points to alienation from the Giver even while receiving gifts.

“Uniting thy glory and man’s happiness” was expressed as finding my happiness in God being honored and loved, preserving the original’s claim that true love refuses to separate human good from God’s glory.
